Q: Semantic HTML, responsive layout and accessible interaction
explain:
A web interface starts with a document: headings establish topic hierarchy, landmarks identify navigation and main content, and form labels connect a question to its control. A button receives keyboard activation and a disabled state from the platform. Replacing it with a clickable div creates extra work for focus, keyboard events and semantics. Use a link to navigate to a resource and a button to change state. Explain validation errors next to their fields and keep user input after a failed request.

Layout needs to tolerate content rather than a particular screenshot. Start with one readable column, a bounded paragraph measure and flexible spacing. A grid can add a second pane when space permits; a preformatted code block may scroll inside its container while ordinary prose wraps. Test long identifiers, translated labels and text enlarged to 200%. A narrow screen should not require horizontal scrolling just to read an explanation. A fixed toolbar must not hide focused controls.

Accessibility is part of the interaction contract. A search dialog must have a name, move focus inside on opening, contain keyboard navigation while active and return focus to the opener. Do not move focus after each generated token. A polite status region can announce transitions such as streaming, failed and complete, while text accumulates in a separate region. Announcing every token overwhelms users. Icons and color can reinforce a status but must not be its only expression.

The local fixture uses a labeled form, scenario selector, actual buttons and a status region. It displays generated-looking text through textContent, preserving literal markup as text. A complete visual answer is intentionally different from the streaming state. Core documentation can remain readable without JavaScript even though the live exercise requires scripting. These guarantees should appear in the acceptance criteria before styling begins, so a later framework migration preserves the same user behavior.
example: A citation inspector opens over an AI response while the user navigates by keyboard. Record which button opened the inspector. Give the dialog a name and move focus to its first useful control. Make background controls inert and close on an explicit button or Escape. Return focus to the opener; preserve the response and scroll position. Result: The user can inspect evidence and resume the original task without losing context.
takeaway: If keyboard activation fails, inspect the element and event path before adding more key handlers. Check the accessible name and focused element; a visible label near a control is not necessarily programmatically associated with it.

Q: JavaScript promises, TypeScript boundaries and React snapshots
explain:
JavaScript executes a synchronous stack of work and resumes asynchronous callbacks through its event loop. Await does not turn a CPU-heavy loop into background work: the loop still blocks the page while it runs. A promise resolving to an HTTP response also does not imply a successful status. Check response.ok, validate the content type and parse the body according to a declared contract. Network failure, an HTTP error, invalid JSON and a valid business rejection need different user-facing recovery paths.

TypeScript describes the values your code expects; it cannot force an external service to obey. Treat received JSON as unknown until a validator has checked required fields, types, bounds and allowed states. A cast such as payload as Result changes the compiler's view, not the payload. Prefer a discriminated union for idle, loading, streaming, complete, failed and cancelled states. It rules out contradictory combinations such as loading=false with a hidden pending approval, but the network decoder still needs real checks.

React rendering is a snapshot of state. An event handler closes over the values from its render; calling a setter schedules another render rather than rewriting that closure. When the next value depends on the previous value, a functional update or reducer avoids losing concurrent updates. Store the minimal authoritative state and derive values such as canSubmit. Avoid separately storing the same response in component state, a cache and a mutable module global with unclear ownership.

Effects synchronize with systems outside rendering, such as a subscription or connection. Return cleanup that unsubscribes or aborts the old operation. Also guard which request owns a response: cancellation can race with an already delivered callback. The fixture's generation counter rejects stale events even after a new request begins. In a React port, keep that ownership token in a ref and drive visible state through a reducer. Keep rendering free of network side effects so repeated renders do not send duplicate work.
example: A user submits request A, quickly submits B, and A finishes last. Assign each submission an increasing generation number. Capture its generation before awaiting work. Accept a response only when its captured generation still matches the active one. Abort A to save work, but retain the generation check because completion may already be queued. Result: B remains visible even if A finishes after its cancellation request.
takeaway: Log a synthetic request ID, render generation and event sequence without recording the prompt. If an older answer overwrites a new one, compare ownership tokens; adding a loading boolean will not establish which request won.

Q: Browser trust boundaries, authentication UX and measured performance
explain:
Treat model text, retrieved passages and tool output as untrusted input. A model can repeat an HTML payload without understanding it. Render plain text by default; if Markdown is required, use an explicit parser and sanitizer configuration and restrict link protocols. Do not concatenate generated text into HTML, inline event handlers or script URLs. A claimed citation needs both a permitted source identity and server-side access control before a real document can be opened.

Authentication UX must explain session expiry and permission denial without exposing data. HttpOnly cookies reduce direct JavaScript access to a session token but require appropriate CSRF defenses and cookie settings. A bearer token held by JavaScript is exposed to successful script injection. Neither storage choice replaces object authorization on the server. After login identity changes, invalidate user-scoped caches and pending responses so one user does not see another user's retained state.

Performance work begins with a user-visible target and a measurement. A fast first token can coexist with a slow final answer, excessive rendering work or a broken cancellation path. Batch incoming updates to avoid rendering once per byte, and bound retained conversation/history. Lazy load large code examples and optional runtimes. A bigger bundle or unnecessary rerender is an engineering trade-off; optimize the measured bottleneck rather than adding memoization to every component.

Use a fixture to measure repeated starts, slow consumers, long text and malformed frames. Record the device/browser, input size, number of updates and timing window so a result can be reproduced. Keep a separate accessibility check because dropping announcements or focus indicators can make an interface seem faster while harming users. Production telemetry should record stage timings and aggregate outcomes without capturing complete prompts, document bodies or credentials by default.
example: A retrieved passage contains an image tag with an event handler. Render the passage as literal text in the fixture. If Markdown is enabled, verify sanitizer policy against the payload. Restrict outgoing citation URLs to supported protocols and permitted source routes. Test after a user switch to prove cached passages are scoped. Result: The passage cannot execute script or become an authorization bypass.
takeaway: If a user reports a previous account response appearing after sign-in, trace identity, cache key and pending request generation together. Purging visible text without invalidating a background request can allow the data to reappear.
